analysis.investment_thesis: Alembic is a 117-year-old pharma house with a loyal promoter and decent gross margins, but nine years of capital deployment have yielded zero earnings growth — net profit in 2025 (₹582 Cr) is actually lower than 2016 (₹720 Cr). Until the heavy capex cycle translates into consistent ROE above 15% and positive free cash flow, this fails my most basic quality screen.
key_strengths: Strong promoter commitment — 69.74% holding, stable and aligned with minority shareholders
Wide gross margin of 71.5% signals real pricing power and formulation mix quality
Debt-to-Equity of 0.28 is within acceptable range and the company has operated with a conservative balance sheet historically
key_risks: Earnings destruction: 9-year net profit CAGR is -2.3%; EBITDA CAGR essentially 0% — capital has been deployed but returns have not materialised
Debt spike in FY25: borrowings surged from ₹513 Cr to ₹1,489 Cr in one year, while OCF collapsed from ₹803 Cr to just ₹88 Cr and FCF turned deeply negative at -₹466 Cr
Finance cost compounding at 35.9% CAGR (₹5 Cr → ₹79 Cr) on a shrinking earnings base — this is the wrong direction entirely
red_flags: ROE of 11.4% and ROCE of 13% — well below my 15% minimum; capital is being destroyed, not compounded
Free cash flow -₹466 Cr in FY25 on ₹564 Cr capex — the capex machine is running but the returns engine is stalled
Net profit peak was ₹1,146 Cr in FY21; four years later it sits at ₹582 Cr — over 49% earnings decline from peak with no clear recovery inflection
Revenue CAGR of only 8.6% over 9 years is below my minimum threshold of 10% for a growth investment
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Alembic Pharmaceuticals is a business I understand — old Indian pharma family, strong promoter, healthcare sector, which I respect. But good industries do not automatically make good investments. The data here tells a sobering story: over nine years, the company grew revenue from ₹3,166 Cr to ₹6,672 Cr (8.6% CAGR), yet net profit actually shrank from ₹720 Cr to ₹582 Cr. Massive capex was deployed — ₹2,000+ Cr over the last 4 years alone, visible in CWIP ballooning to ₹2,304 Cr at peak — building US FDA-compliant plants and injectable capacity. The market rewarded this vision in 2021 when profits hit ₹1,146 Cr. But FY22 onwards has been a painful reversal, with USFDA compliance costs, pricing pressure in US generics, and rising debt eroding what was once a capital-light model.

FY25 is particularly alarming for a conservative investor like me: borrowings nearly tripled in one year to ₹1,489 Cr, OCF collapsed from ₹803 Cr to ₹88 Cr, and FCF turned to -₹466 Cr. The forward P/E of 18.55x implies the market expects a sharp earnings recovery — and that may well happen if US formulation approvals accelerate. But I do not invest in hopes and turnaround stories. I need demonstrated, consistent compounding. At P/E 23x on shrinking profits, ROE of 11.4%, and negative FCF, there is no margin of safety here. I would rather wait on the sidelines and pay a higher price after the business proves its recovery is real and durable.
